---
title: Writing files
guide-section: "Using the output"
---

A study's datasets are available in memory as DataFrames (`Study.sdtm`, `Study.adam`), and can be
written to files the way a sponsor would deliver them. Writing needs no DataFrame backend: the
files are encoded by the Rust engine, so a script that only writes files runs without Polars,
pandas or PyArrow installed.

```{python}
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import trialforge as tf

trial = tf.study("parallel_continuous", n=100, seed=1)
out = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
```

## A submission package

`Study.write_submission()` writes `sdtm/` and `adam/` folders, each with one SAS transport (XPT v5)
file per dataset and a Define-XML 2.1 `define.xml`, plus the [truth manifest](05-truth.qmd) as
`truth.json`:

```{python}
written = trial.write_submission(out / "submission")
sorted(str(p.relative_to(out)) for p in written)
```

This is the layout of the data part of a regulatory submission (module 5 of the eCTD keeps SDTM and
ADaM in separate folders, each with its define.xml), so it is what a validator or a reviewer's tool
expects to be pointed at. The folder is created if needed, and existing files with the same names
are overwritten.

## Other formats

`Study.write()` writes every dataset into one directory, in one or more formats (XPT by default):

```{python}
tf.formats()
```

```{python}
written = trial.write(out / "files", formats=["csv", "dataset-json"])
sorted(p.name for p in written)[:6]
```

Files are named by the lower-case dataset name, such as `dm.xpt`, with SDTM and ADaM side by side.
`truth.json` is written with them, and a study with [defects](09-defects.qmd) also gets
`defects.json`. `write()` doesn't write define.xml; use `write_submission()` or `define_xml()`
(below) for that.

## What each format contains

The formats differ in how much of the metadata they carry and in how they encode types and
missing values. In memory, every column has one of five types: character, numeric (floating
point), integer, date or datetime.

| | XPT v5 | CSV | Dataset-JSON 1.1 | Parquet |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dataset and variable labels | Yes | No | Yes | Yes, as field metadata |
| Character | Blank-padded to the longest value | Text, quoted when needed | `string` with its `length` | `Utf8` |
| Numeric and integer | 8-byte IBM floating point | Shortest round-trip form | `double` and `integer` | `Float64` and `Int64` |
| Date | SAS date (days since 1960-01-01), `DATE9.` format | `YYYY-MM-DD` | `date`: ISO 8601 text, `targetDataType` `integer` | `Date32` |
| Datetime | SAS datetime (seconds since 1960-01-01), `DATETIME20.` format | `YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm`, with seconds if not zero | `datetime`: ISO 8601 text, `targetDataType` `integer` | `Timestamp` (milliseconds) |
| Missing | Blank (character) or `.` (numeric) | Empty field | `null` | Null |

SDTM dates (`--DTC`) are always character, ISO 8601 text that may carry a clock time;
only ADaM has date and datetime types (`ADT`, `TRTSDT`, `ADTM`).

### XPT v5

SAS transport version 5 is the format the FDA and PMDA require for submitted datasets. It is old
and strict, and trialforge's metadata is authored within its limits:

- dataset and variable names of at most 8 characters, and labels of at most 40;
- character values of at most 200 bytes, in ASCII;
- one dataset per file, as submissions expect.

The length of a character variable is the length of its longest value in the study, as the FDA's
technical conformance guide asks, so the same variable can have different lengths in two studies.

### CSV

One file per dataset with a header row of variable names, following RFC 4180. CSV has no types or
labels, so it suits quick inspection and tools that read text; prefer one of the other formats when
types matter.

### Dataset-JSON 1.1

CDISC's JSON exchange format: one file per dataset holding its label, column metadata (name, label,
type, length and key sequence) and rows. The file and item OIDs match those in define.xml, and
`metaDataRef` points at it.

### Parquet

Apache Parquet, one file per dataset, with the dataset name and label in the schema metadata and
each variable's label in its field metadata. Polars, pandas, PyArrow, DuckDB and Spark all read it.

## Reading files back

Each format reads back with the usual tools. Polars restores Parquet's types, including dates:

```{python}
import polars as pl

trial.write(out / "parquet", formats=["parquet"])
pl.read_parquet(out / "parquet" / "adsl.parquet").select("USUBJID", "TRTSDT", "TRTEDT").head(3)
```

XPT is read by `pandas.read_sas()`, haven's `read_xpt()` in R, pyreadstat and SAS itself. pandas
returns dates as SAS day numbers, without applying the `DATE9.` format; convert them with the SAS
epoch:

```{python}
import pandas as pd

adsl = pd.read_sas(out / "submission" / "adam" / "adsl.xpt", format="xport", encoding="ascii")
adsl["TRTSDT"] = pd.to_datetime(adsl["TRTSDT"], unit="D", origin="1960-01-01")
adsl[["USUBJID", "TRTSDT", "AGE"]].head(3)
```

## Define-XML

Each `define.xml` documents one standard's datasets. It is built from trialforge's metadata (labels,
origins, derivation methods and codelists) and from the data itself (lengths, data types and the
terms that actually occur), so it describes this study rather than a template:

- **Standards**: the implementation guide (SDTMIG 3.4 or ADaMIG 1.3) and the CDISC Controlled
Terminology version.
- **Datasets** (`ItemGroupDef`): each dataset's class, structure, keys and a link to its XPT file.
- **Variables** (`ItemDef`): name, label, data type, length, and origin: collected, derived,
assigned or from the protocol in SDTM, and derived, assigned or carried from a predecessor (with its
source variable) in ADaM.
- **Codelists** (`CodeList`): the controlled terms each variable uses, limited to the terms present
in the data, and a sponsor codelist of `PARAMCD`{.gd-no-link} values with their decodes.
- **Value-level metadata** (`ValueListDef`, `WhereClauseDef`): results by test code in LB and VS
and `AVAL`{.gd-no-link} by parameter in the BDS datasets, each with its own type and length.
- **Methods** (`MethodDef`): for ADaM, how each derived variable is computed, in the words of the
derivation.

## define.xml as text

`Study.define_xml()` returns the Define-XML 2.1 document for either standard as a string, without
writing anything:

```{python}
print(trial.define_xml("adam")[:600])
```

A derivation method, for example:

```{python}
adam_define = trial.define_xml("adam")
start = adam_define.find('<MethodDef OID="MT.ADSL.AGEGR1"')
print(adam_define[start : adam_define.find("</MethodDef>", start) + len("</MethodDef>")])
```

## Deterministic files

Writing the same study twice gives byte-identical files. The creation timestamps that XPT,
Dataset-JSON and define.xml carry are set to the study's data cutoff rather than the time of writing,
and nothing else depends on the machine or the clock. So you can check files into version control,
compare them with a checksum, or regenerate them later and get the same bytes (see
[Reproducibility](11-reproducibility.qmd)).

## DataFrames

`Study.sdtm` and `Study.adam` are dictionaries of DataFrames of the `output` type you chose in
`tf.study()`: Polars (the default), pandas or PyArrow. Columns keep their SDTM and ADaM types:
dates in SDTM are ISO 8601 text (`--DTC`), and ADaM dates and datetimes are proper date types.

```{python}
pandas_trial = tf.study("parallel_continuous", n=100, seed=1, output="pandas")
pandas_trial.adam["ADSL"][["USUBJID", "TRT01P", "TRTSDT", "TRTEDT"]].head()
```

The DataFrames are built when you first access `Study.sdtm` or `Study.adam` and then kept, so
looking at a study costs nothing until you do. With PyArrow, each table carries the dataset and
variable labels in its schema metadata, as Parquet files do.
